cemc-hypatia-2011-01a.title: Slope and intercept
cemc-hypatia-2011-01a.body:
$D$ is the midpoint of $AB$, so $D = (0, 3)$. The slope of $CD$ is $\frac{3 - 0}{0 - 8} = -\frac38$, and the $y$-intercept is $3$ (the line passes through $D$ on the $y$-axis).

**Answer: $y = -\frac38 x + 3$**

cemc-hypatia-2011-01a.title: Intercept form
cemc-hypatia-2011-01a.body:
The line meets the $x$-axis at $C(8, 0)$ and the $y$-axis at $D(0, 3)$, so its equation is $\frac{x}{8} + \frac{y}{3} = 1$, i.e. $3x + 8y = 24$.

**Answer: $3x + 8y = 24$, i.e. $y = -\frac38x + 3$**

cemc-hypatia-2011-01b.title: Intersect the lines
cemc-hypatia-2011-01b.body:
$E = (4, 0)$, so line $AE$ has slope $\frac{6-0}{0-4} = -\frac32$ and equation $y = -\frac32 x + 6$.

Setting $-\frac38 x + 3 = -\frac32 x + 6$ and multiplying by $8$: $-3x + 24 = -12x + 48$, so $9x = 24$ and $x = \frac83$. Then $y = -\frac32 \cdot \frac83 + 6 = 2$.

**Answer: $F = (\frac83, 2)$**

cemc-hypatia-2011-01b.title: Centroid
cemc-hypatia-2011-01b.body:
$AE$ and $CD$ are two medians of $\triangle ABC$, so $F$ is the centroid, the average of the vertices:
$$F = \left(\frac{0 + 0 + 8}{3}, \frac{6 + 0 + 0}{3}\right) = \left(\frac83, 2\right).$$

**Answer: $(\frac83, 2)$**

cemc-hypatia-2011-01c.title: Base and height
cemc-hypatia-2011-01c.body:
$\triangle DBC$ has base $BC = 8$ and height $BD = 3$, so its area is $\frac12 \cdot 8 \cdot 3 = 12$.

**Answer: 12**

cemc-hypatia-2011-01c.title: Half of the big triangle
cemc-hypatia-2011-01c.body:
$D$ is the midpoint of $AB$, so $\triangle DBC$ has the same base $BC$ as $\triangle ABC$ and half the height. Its area is half of $\frac12 \cdot 8 \cdot 6 = 24$, which is $12$.

**Answer: 12**

cemc-hypatia-2011-01d.title: Subtract a triangle
cemc-hypatia-2011-01d.body:
Area $DBEF$ = area $\triangle DBC$ − area $\triangle FEC$. Triangle $FEC$ has base $EC = 4$ and height equal to the $y$-coordinate of $F$, which is $2$, so its area is $\frac12 \cdot 4 \cdot 2 = 4$.

Area $DBEF = 12 - 4 = 8$.

**Answer: 8**

cemc-hypatia-2011-01d.title: Medians make six equal pieces
cemc-hypatia-2011-01d.body:
The three medians of a triangle cut it into six small triangles of equal area. Quadrilateral $DBEF$ consists of two of these six pieces (the pieces $DBF$ and $BEF$, where $BF$ lies along the third median). Since $\triangle ABC$ has area $24$, the quadrilateral has area $\frac26 \cdot 24 = 8$.

**Answer: 8**

cemc-hypatia-2011-02a.title: Count the ones digits
cemc-hypatia-2011-02a.body:
The ones digit can be any of $1, 2, \dots, 8$ (8 choices), except $3$, since $33$ is a multiple of $11$. That leaves $7$ numbers: $31, 32, 34, 35, 36, 37, 38$.

**Answer: 7**

cemc-hypatia-2011-02a.title: List them
cemc-hypatia-2011-02a.body:
The numbers $31$ to $38$ avoid $0$ and $9$; among them only $33$ is a multiple of $11$. So $8 - 1 = 7$.

**Answer: 7**

cemc-hypatia-2011-02b.title: Count the tens digits
cemc-hypatia-2011-02b.body:
The tens digit can be $1, \dots, 8$, except $8$ (since $88 = 8 \times 11$). That leaves $7$ numbers: $18, 28, 38, 48, 58, 68, 78$.

**Answer: 7**

cemc-hypatia-2011-02b.title: Same idea as (a)
cemc-hypatia-2011-02b.body:
A two-digit number with nonzero digits is a multiple of $11$ exactly when its two digits are equal. So for any fixed ones digit from $1$ to $8$, exactly one of the $8$ possible tens digits is excluded, leaving $7$.

**Answer: 7**

cemc-hypatia-2011-02c.title: Total minus multiples of 11
cemc-hypatia-2011-02c.body:
Ignoring the multiple-of-11 rule, there are $8 \times 8 = 64$ numbers with both digits in $1, \dots, 8$. The multiples of $11$ among them are $11, 22, \dots, 88$ (8 numbers). So $|S| = 64 - 8 = 56$.

**Answer: 56**

cemc-hypatia-2011-02c.title: Digit by digit
cemc-hypatia-2011-02c.body:
Choose the tens digit ($8$ ways), then a ones digit from $1$–$8$ different from the tens digit ($7$ ways). That gives $8 \times 7 = 56$.

**Answer: 56**

cemc-hypatia-2011-02d.title: Sum digits by place
cemc-hypatia-2011-02d.body:
From (a) and (b), each digit $1, \dots, 8$ appears as the tens digit of exactly $7$ numbers of $S$ and as the ones digit of exactly $7$ numbers.

Since $1 + 2 + \dots + 8 = 36$, the ones digits add to $7 \times 36 = 252$ and the tens digits contribute $10 \times 7 \times 36 = 2520$. The total is $2520 + 252 = 2772$.

**Answer: 2772**

cemc-hypatia-2011-02d.title: All minus excluded
cemc-hypatia-2011-02d.body:
The $64$ numbers with both digits in $1$–$8$ have sum $8 \cdot 10 \cdot 36 + 8 \cdot 36 = 2880 + 288 = 3168$ (each digit appears $8$ times in each place). Subtract the multiples of $11$: $11 + 22 + \dots + 88 = 11 \cdot 36 = 396$. So the sum is $3168 - 396 = 2772$.

**Answer: 2772**

cemc-hypatia-2011-03a.title: General form
cemc-hypatia-2011-03a.body:
Let $3x = 5y = 2z = k$. Then $k$ is divisible by $3$, $5$ and $2$, hence by $30$: $k = 30m$, so $(x, y, z) = (10m, 6m, 15m)$. With $x = 50$, $m = 5$, giving $y = 30$ and $z = 75$.

**Answer: $y = 30$, $z = 75$**

cemc-hypatia-2011-03b.title: Divisibility
cemc-hypatia-2011-03b.body:
Since $3x = 5y$, $3$ divides $5y$; as $\gcd(3, 5) = 1$, $3 \mid y$.
Since $2z = 5y$, $2$ divides $5y$; as $\gcd(2, 5) = 1$, $2 \mid y$.
So $y$ is divisible by $\operatorname{lcm}(2, 3) = 6$. ∎

cemc-hypatia-2011-03b.title: Parametrize
cemc-hypatia-2011-03b.body: As in part (a), the common value $k = 3x = 5y = 2z$ is a multiple of $3$, $5$ and $2$, so $k = 30m$ for a positive integer $m$. Then $y = k/5 = 6m$ is divisible by $6$. ∎

cemc-hypatia-2011-03c.title: Divide each variable
cemc-hypatia-2011-03c.body:
As in (b): from $3x = 5y$ and $3x = 2z$, $5 \mid 3x$ and $2 \mid 3x$, so $10 \mid x$. From $2z = 3x$ and $2z = 5y$, $3 \mid 2z$ and $5 \mid 2z$, so $15 \mid z$. And $6 \mid y$ by part (b).

Therefore $xyz$ is divisible by $10 \cdot 6 \cdot 15 = 900$. ∎

cemc-hypatia-2011-03c.title: Parametrize
cemc-hypatia-2011-03c.body: Every Trenti-triple has the form $(x, y, z) = (10m, 6m, 15m)$ for a positive integer $m$ (part (a)). Then $xyz = 900 m^3$, which is divisible by $900$. ∎

cemc-hypatia-2011-04a.title: Sort by number of 1s
cemc-hypatia-2011-04a.body:
After removing the $1$s, the remaining parts are odd numbers $\ge 3$:
- no 1s: parts $\ge 3$ summing to $8$: $3 + 5$
- one 1: summing to $7$: $7$
- two 1s: summing to $6$: $3 + 3$
- three 1s: summing to $5$: $5$
- five 1s: summing to $3$: $3$
- eight 1s: nothing left

With four, six or seven 1s the remainder ($4$, $2$, $1$) cannot be made from odd parts $\ge 3$. That is $6$ ways, so $F(8) = 6$.

cemc-hypatia-2011-04b.title: Add a 1, then find one more
cemc-hypatia-2011-04b.body:
Call a way of writing $n$ as a sum of odd positive integers a *representation*. Adding a term $1$ to each representation of $n$ gives a representation of $n + 1$; different representations of $n$ give different ones of $n + 1$ (remove the extra $1$ to recover the original). So $F(n + 1) \ge F(n)$, and all these representations contain a $1$.

We find a representation of $n + 1$ with **no** $1$:
- If $n + 1$ is odd: the single term $n + 1$ (which is not $1$ since $n > 3$).
- If $n + 1$ is even: then $n$ is odd and $n \ge 5$, so $n - 2$ is odd and $\ge 3$; use $(n - 2) + 3$.

This representation is not among the $F(n)$ above, so $F(n + 1) \ge F(n) + 1 > F(n)$. ∎

cemc-hypatia-2011-04c.title: Official idea: combine pieces
cemc-hypatia-2011-04c.body:
For a representation of $n$, let $a_n$ be "$n$ ones", let $b_n$ be $(n-1) + 1$ if $n$ is even and $(n - 2) + 1 + 1$ if $n$ is odd, and let $S_n$ be the list of the other $F(n) - 2$ representations of $n$ (for $n > 3$, $a_n \ne b_n$).

Joining two representations of $n$ gives one of $2n$. Consider
- $a_n + s$ for each $s \in S_n$ ($F(n) - 2$ of them),
- $b_n + s$ for each $s \in S_n$ ($F(n) - 2$ of them),
- $a_n + a_n$, $a_n + b_n$, $b_n + b_n$,
- $(2n - 1) + 1$ and $(2n - 3) + 3$.

That is $2(F(n) - 2) + 5 = 2F(n) + 1$ representations. They are distinct:
- The last two contain a part $2n - 1$ or $2n - 3$, which is larger than $n$ (as $n > 3$), while all the others have all parts $\le n$.
- Within each family the representations are distinct, and $a_n + a_n$, $a_n + b_n$, $b_n + b_n$ are different from each other and (by the definition of $S_n$) from the first two families.
- If one representation were in both $a_n + S_n$ and $b_n + S_n$, it would contain $n$ ones and also the part $n - 1$ or $n - 2$; these already add to $2n - 1$ or $2n - 2$, so the remainder is $1$ or $1 + 1$, i.e. it is exactly $a_n + b_n$ — which would force the $S_n$ piece to be $b_n$ or $a_n$, impossible.

So $F(2n) \ge 2F(n) + 1 > 2F(n)$. ∎

cemc-hypatia-2011-04c.title: Split by the number of 1s
cemc-hypatia-2011-04c.body:
**Many 1s.** Representations of $2n$ with at least $n$ ones correspond exactly to representations of $n$ (remove $n$ ones / add $n$ ones). So there are exactly $F(n)$ of them.

**Few 1s.** Given a representation $\lambda$ of $n$ with $k$ ones, let $N$ be its parts other than $1$ (they are odd, $\ge 3$, and sum to $n - k$). Map $\lambda$ to the representation of $2n$
$$\Phi(\lambda) = N \cup \{n + k\} \text{ if } n + k \text{ is odd},\qquad N \cup \{n + k - 1,\ 1\} \text{ if } n + k \text{ is even}.$$
The parts add to $(n - k) + (n + k) = 2n$, and $\Phi(\lambda)$ has at most one $1$, so fewer than $n$ ones.

$\Phi$ is one-to-one: the new big part $L$ ($= n + k$ or $n + k - 1$) is at least as large as every part of $N$ (if $k \ge 1$ then $L \ge n > n - k$; if $k = 0$ and $n$ is odd then $L = n$; if $k = 0$ and $n$ is even then every part of $N$ is at most $n - 3 < L$). So from $\Phi(\lambda)$ we read $L$ as the largest part, decide $n + k = L$ or $L + 1$ by whether a $1$ is present, recover $k$, remove $L$ (and the $1$) to get $N$, and add back $k$ ones.

So there are at least $F(n)$ representations of $2n$ with fewer than $n$ ones of this form.

**One more.** Every $\Phi(\lambda)$ has at most one $1$ and a part $\ge n - 1$. Write $2n = 3q + r$ with $r \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ and take $q$ threes and $r$ ones. It has fewer than $n$ ones. If $r = 2$ it has two ones; if $r \le 1$ then $n \ge 5$ (since $8 = 3 \cdot 2 + 2$) and its largest part $3 < n - 1$. Either way it is not of the form $\Phi(\lambda)$.

Hence $F(2n) \ge F(n) + F(n) + 1 > 2F(n)$. ∎
